evidence_quotes.quote: This study aims to identify illustrative cases that leveraged policy and systems change through existing policies and programs in communities to mitigate contaminants including lead, nitrates and arsenic to increase access to safe home drinking water from public or private sources.

evidence_quotes.page: PMC PMC10818245 - Cincinnati’s Enhanced Lead Program
evidence_quotes.quote: Local ordinances prohibiting private lead service lines and providing local financing and subsidies for private lead service line replacements in collaboration with the public water system.

evidence_quotes.page: PMC PMC10818245 - New Jersey Private Well Testing Act
evidence_quotes.quote: State policy requiring home well water quality testing when a property is sold and every five years for rental properties served by wells.
Researchers estimated the projected 5-year population reach and costs of implementing each policy or program in the geographic area according to the eligibility criteria of the specific case studied.
The research team interviewed 16 key informants (100 percent of those invited) using snowball sampling from a primary informant.

Average annual cost per household that received information about their water quality ranged from $75 to $2,780. Data presented by payer (in several categories) suggest that the household’s average annual cost would range from $0.12 to $1,590, depending on the strategy.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access to safe drinking water across community water systems and private domestic wells, recording specifically drinking-water quality mitigation (lead, arsenic and nitrates), private-side lead service line replacement, point-of-use filtration/bottled water provision and household affordability. Exclusion 3 (water-quality studies not examining access or governance) does not apply because both equitable access/affordability and policy/governance mechanisms are directly analyzed.
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading are satisfied, though borderline under the narrow reading. Under the plain wording, the study evaluates six state, municipal, utility and WIC policies and programs for safe home drinking water. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although four cases involve programmatic testing/filter delivery and detailed legal case profiles appeared in a companion study (Wilking et al., 2022), this paper directly models rule-type mechanisms governing household safe-water access and affordability: (1) local ordinances prohibiting private lead service lines combined with municipal financing and subsidies for private-side replacement (Cincinnati), (2) a state statutory mandate requiring well testing at property sale and every 5 years for rental tenure without treatment subsidies (New Jersey), (3) means-tested WIC eligibility screening versus universal utility or tenure-based rules governing reach to low-income families, and (4) cost-sharing rules across payers determining household out-of-pocket burden.
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical mixed-methods multiple-case economic evaluation combining 16 semi-structured key informant interviews, review of utility, regulatory and program budget documents, and national/local demographic and housing data (US American Housing Survey, WIC/SNAP) in an activity-based micro-costing framework. Lack of a regression effect size pertains only to meta-analysis gating (Criterion 6 in INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md), not systematic-review eligibility.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports outcomes directly relevant to access, water quality and affordability at the household level: projected 5-year eligible population reach (including share of low-income households with young children from 4-26% in broad strategies to 100% in WIC-screened strategies), estimated household adoption of safe-water mitigation or lead service line replacement (62-80% based on empirical program uptake), and average annual cost borne by individual households ($0.12 to $1,590 per year).
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and unit of analysis (US households, focusing on low-income families with young children aged 0-5 years across 6 local/state jurisdictions), exposures (6 legal, utility and WIC-screened safe-water strategies), outcomes (population reach, mitigation adoption and annual/5-year costs by activity and payer) and study design (mixed-methods multiple-case activity-based costing economic evaluation).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Mixed-methods multiple-case study and activity-based micro-costing economic evaluation (16 key informant interviews, administrative/regulatory document review and 5-year cost and population-reach projections)
population_and_sample: Households (specifically low-income families with young children aged 0-5 years) across 6 US state and local case-study jurisdictions (New Jersey; New Hampshire and Vermont; New Hampshire statewide; Porterville, California; Cincinnati, Ohio; and Denver, Colorado), informed by 16 key informant interviews and US American Housing Survey / WIC data
exposure: Six state and local safe home drinking-water policies and programs differing in legal mandates, eligibility screening and payer cost-sharing rules: New Jersey Private Well Testing Act (mandatory testing at property sale and every 5 years for rentals), Cincinnati ordinances prohibiting private lead service lines with local financing/subsidies, WIC means-tested testing/filtration/bottled-water programs in New Hampshire and Porterville (CA), Denver Water utility filter distribution for lead service lines, and NH/VT clinic-based infant well testing
outcome: Projected 5-year household reach (receipt of water-quality information among eligible households and low-income families with young children), household adoption of contaminant mitigation strategies including filtration, bottled water or lead service line replacement (62-80%), and 5-year and average annual costs overall, by activity and borne out-of-pocket by households ($0.12 to $1,590 per household per year; affordability)
rationale: This empirical mixed-methods multiple-case economic evaluation examines six US state and local policies and programs aimed at increasing household access to safe drinking water (mitigating lead, arsenic and nitrates across public water systems and private domestic wells) for low-income families with young children. Although borderline because four cases focus on clinic, WIC or utility testing/filter delivery and detailed legal analysis appeared in a companion report, the study satisfies both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 by evaluating rule-type mechanisms governing access and household cost burden—including municipal ordinances prohibiting private lead service lines with financing/subsidies (Cincinnati), a state statutory well-testing mandate triggered by property sale and 5-year rental tenure without remediation subsidies (New Jersey), means-tested WIC eligibility screening (New Hampshire, Porterville) and payer cost-sharing rules—against empirical reach, mitigation adoption (62-80%) and household affordability outcomes ($0.12 to $1,590 annual household cost).
